1:
The placing of the passage is treated as deliberate. Gill argues the words were spoken before the firstborn were slain and probably before the three days' darkness, since the command must have come four days before the passover; he would render the opening as the Lord had spoken, and holds the account was deferred here so the plague history should not be interrupted. Keil reads in the land of Egypt as connecting this law with the giving of the law at Sinai, and explains why the feast had to come first: a divine consecration was necessary, so that the outward severance from Egypt might be matched by an inward severance from everything heathen, laying the foundation of Israel's birth into a new life of grace.

Whether a new calendar was instituted here is disputed. Clarke states the common view, that God now moved the year's commencement from Tisri, the month in which the Jews suppose the world was created with the earth at once in all its fruits, to Abib, giving a twofold reckoning. He then reports the objection and calls it plausible: eminently learned men dispute it, especially Houbigant, who contends that no new commencement is noted here, since the year had always begun in this month and the words shall be have nothing answering to them in the Hebrew; he renders it as a statement, this month is to you the head of the months, God marking it only so posterity might know when to keep the passover. Ellicott gives the opposite account, that the Hebrews had begun with Tisri near the autumnal equinox, following neither the Egyptian custom of beginning in June with the Nile's rise nor the Babylonian at the vernal equinox, and that henceforth they kept two years, the first civil month being the seventh sacred. The month, he notes, was still called Abib, the month of greenness. Gill adds an agricultural check, that the name means an ear of corn and the barley was then in ear, which shows in what month these things were transacted. Henry and Wesley put it in round terms, from mid September to mid March, at least in ecclesiastical computations; Henry finds it good to begin the year, and especially our lives, with God.

The interval is explained practically. Clarke observes that in later times preparation began on the thirteenth, but this first occasion required more time amid very great confusion; and he passes on Ainsworth's remark that Israel afterwards crossed Jordan, and Christ entered Jerusalem, on this day. Ellicott gives the reason from the thing itself: the instruction must have issued some days before the tenth, to allow time for careful inspection so that entire freedom from blemish might be ascertained. Both note that the word rendered lamb is vague, applied equally to sheep and goats; Ellicott adds that sex and age were fixed later while this ambiguity remained, and that the command presupposes a society without extreme poverty, every Israelite able to own or buy one. Keil explains that all the congregation means the nation represented by its elders, and reckoning by fathers' houses the natural distribution into families, so that one household circle should unite and not an indiscriminate company.

Calvin raises the question the arrangement provokes. If one Lamb alone reconciled the Church, why command a lamb slain in every house, as though there were a special sacrifice for each? His answer is that although all were protected by the same blood and one rite united them in one expiation, God would have every family separately reminded, feeling the grace more peculiarly conferred on itself, as baptism is one yet conferred on every individual. The joining of neighbours he explains by the rule that nothing be left, the whole being consumed lest the sacred feast be mixed with daily food, or superstition creep in from the remnants, for which cause even the bones were burnt.
4:
The rule for joining households is a calculation. Keil takes the clause literally as the house being too small for a lamb, and explains that families deciding whether to unite were to estimate how much each person would eat, so that more than two might join. Ellicott describes the same from the other side, two small families clubbing together or a large one drafting off members to make up a small one, and corrects the English to shall ye count, admitting more or fewer as they were likely to eat less or more. Both give the traditional bounds, Clarke from the rabbins and Ellicott from Josephus, that ten was the least sufficient number and twenty not too many.

On soundness they divide between contempt and precision. Gill reports that Maimonides reckons fifty blemishes, any one making a creature unfit. Clarke reports the same figure and despises it, saying the rabbins have trifled most egregiously, itemising five in the ear, three in the eyelid, eight in the eye, three in the nose, six in the mouth. Ellicott appeals to a principle, that natural piety forbids offering the blind, the lame or the sick and requires giving God our best; and he holds males especially appropriate, the victim representing the firstborn male of each house.

The age of the animal produces a flat disagreement. Clarke glosses a male of the first year as any age between eight days and twelve months. Keil rejects precisely that gloss, the rule about standing in the first year applying to other sacrifices only; his rendering is simply one year old, and Ellicott agrees with not above a year old, adding that as children are most innocent when young, so even animals were thought to be. Keil also disposes of the view that oxen were admitted later, calling it quite erroneous and denying it can be proved from the passages cited. Both note that the Hebrew allowed either sheep or goats, Clarke adding that the Hebrews generally preferred the lamb.

Calvin reads the perfection as a measure of what was needed. The people were reminded that the expiation was not legitimate unless it possessed the utmost perfection, such as is never found in men; propitiating God required a more excellent price than the whole human race could furnish, and since such excellency could much less exist in a beast, the celestial purity of Christ was shown forth by the lamb's visible perfection. He then declines an allegory his own tradition offered, preferring to be ignorant why the flesh was roasted and not boiled rather than invent such unfounded subtleties as that Christ was in a manner roasted on the cross.

Why the animal was chosen four days early nobody settles. Keil canvasses the answers: Jonathan and Rashi restricted the rule to the passover in Egypt; Fagius held that the sight of the lamb would prompt conversation about the deliverance, which Keil grants has some truth but says hardly explains exactly four days; and Hoffmann referred it to the four generations since Israel came into Egypt, a suggestion whose probability depends on the lamb being a sacrifice, which Hoffmann himself denies without sufficient reason. Ellicott answers plainly, that the phrase means having it in custody so it could be thoroughly inspected. Clarke lists the four things the rabbins say were required at the first passover only: eating it in houses dispersed through Goshen, taking the lamb on the tenth, striking the blood on the posts, and eating in haste. Gill takes the keeping up as a type of Christ preserved in his infancy.

On the killing Clarke adds two practical points: any person might kill it, the sacrificial act not being confined to the priests, and in the evening is literally between the two evenings, the first from noon to sunset and the second through twilight, so that God sets no particular hour.
7:
The doorway stands for the house. Keil observes that the posts and lintel surrounded the door, and the doorway stood for the house itself, as in thy gates stands for in thy towns; the threshold, which belongs to the door as much as the lintel, was not to be smeared. Clarke supplies Ainsworth's reason, to teach a reverent regard for the blood of Christ, that men should not tread under foot the Son of God. Ellicott adds an archaeological guess about the upper member: the word seems to derive from a root meaning to look out, and to mean the latticed window above the door through which callers were reconnoitred, a feature frequent on early Egyptian monuments; blood made conspicuous there would show atonement had been made for the inmates.

Why roasting was commanded is answered two ways. Clarke notes that it was the ordinary custom to boil, so some think the command was aimed at the Egyptians, who ate raw flesh in honour of Osiris; the Ethiopians, he adds, are still remarkable for it. Ellicott gives homelier reasons, that roasting is the simplest and most primitive mode of cooking meat and the only one open to all, since most would not possess a cauldron large enough for an entire lamb. Keil settles the philology, that the Hebrew behind boiled means to become done rather than to be boiled, and follows Rashi in taking the animal undivided, no bone broken, the viscera roasted in the belly once cleansed.

The prohibition of raw flesh puzzles Gill, who canvasses three readings. Jarchi and Maimonides take the word of flesh the fire has begun to work on but which is not roasted enough to eat; others derive it from a root meaning to break, so that the rule forbids cutting the animal up; and Abarbinel takes it as now, which Gill dismisses as needless since they had already been told to keep the lamb till the fourteenth. Wesley glosses it briefly as half roasted rather than thoroughly dressed. Clarke explains the inclusion of the inward parts by a further polemic, that the heathens abused these for divination and could not once they were roasted thus; Ellicott reports from Justin Martyr the two wooden spits, one perpendicular and one transverse, that extended the lamb on a sort of cross.

The rule that nothing remain draws Clarke into antiquity. From the passover, he argues, the heathens borrowed the sacrifice they called propter viam, offered before a journey and eaten whole if possible, the rest burned; and he retails Cato's jibe, from Macrobius, against a man who having eaten up all his goods set fire to his house, that he had offered his sacrifice propter viam because he burned what he could not eat. His own reason is to prevent putrefaction, since what is offered to God should not see corruption, and he draws the parallel that the Lord's body saw none. Ellicott gives a different reason, that there be neither profanation nor superstitious use of what was left, comparing his own church's rule for the eucharistic elements. Gill turns it typologically, that a whole Christ is to be fed upon by faith.

The travelling posture is agreed to be exceptional. Ellicott states that these injunctions are not repeated later in the law and were not held binding at any passover after the first, referring wholly to the impending departure; Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan saying the same, at this time and not in ages following. Clarke explains each item from Chardin: the loose eastern garment was tucked into the girdle for a journey, and easterns throw off their shoes to eat, since sitting cross-legged makes backless slippers troublesome and they would soil the carpets, so that shoes on the feet is mentioned because it was not customary. Keil reads the costume the same way and glosses the phrase for haste as anxious flight.
12:
The threat against the gods of Egypt is the hardest clause, and Clarke works through three answers, rejecting two. The first, that Egypt's sacred animals made the slaying of their firstborn beasts a judgment on their gods, he finds not very clear or satisfactory. The second, the marginal princes, he answers with a question: did not the judgments fall equally on all Egyptian families, multitudes of whom had no part in the counsel against the Hebrews, so why distinguish some in a calamity all shared? The third is Houbigant's emendation, that the word for gods is a mistake for the word for tents, two letters having been interchanged, giving a threat that not one dwelling in Egypt should be exempted; Clarke calls this simple and natural. Then he undercuts his own preference: however probable the criticism appears, no ancient version supports it and no manuscript collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, and the parallel passage is rather against it. He closes with the principle that a conquered nation's gods were always supposed to have abandoned it or been overcome.

Ellicott takes the opposite line, that gods is far preferable to princes. Some sacred animals were regarded as actual incarnations of deity, so if any perished the threat was executed to the letter; and even apart from that, since cows, goats, cats, dogs, jackals, crocodiles, hippopotami, apes, ibises and frogs were sacred throughout Egypt or in parts of it, a general destruction of firstborn animals would be felt as a blow to the gods almost equally. He also prefers go through to pass through, the verb being entirely unconnected with the word behind passover. Calvin agrees on substance, that God declares himself judge against the false gods because it then appeared how unable they were to help and how vain their service was, and holds he would conquer not the nation only but its very gods; the rabbinic account he calls tame and far-fetched. Both he and Clarke find an allusion to it in the prophet's vision of the Lord coming into Egypt while its idols are moved at his presence.

Whom the blood was a token to is disputed. Gill makes it a sign to Israel that the Lord would make good his promises and to the destroying angel not to enter; Clarke likewise calls it the sign to that angel that the house is under God's protection. Ellicott reverses the direction, rendering it the blood shall be for a token for you, that is, a token to God on their behalf. Keil takes it as a sign and pledge that Jehovah would spare them, and cautions against rendering the last clause for the destroyer, since the noun has no article.

The perpetuity of the ordinance is where they show their hands. Keil grounds it in proportion: an act of redemption of eternal significance requires a commemoration upheld as long as Israel exists as the redeemed people. Clarke calls it an endless statute because representative of the Lamb of God, whose mediation endures while time lasts; and he observes what has happened, that though Jewish sacrifice has wholly ceased the passover and unleavened bread are still kept everywhere, with no lamb offered, the flesh even partly roasted and partly boiled so as not to resemble the primitive sacrifice, since it is held unlawful to sacrifice out of Jerusalem. Calvin restricts the term, admitting perpetuity is meant but only such as would last until the renovation of the Church, as with circumcision and the whole ceremonial law; by Christ's coming it was abolished in use yet only then attained its true solidity, the new covenant destroying the old not in substance but in form. Ellicott makes the continuation concrete, the passover continued in the Eucharist and Easter corresponding exactly in time. Gill notes the Jewish saying that as Israel was redeemed in Nisan, in Nisan they will be redeemed again.
15:
All of them insist on two feasts, not one. Gill holds the seven days of unleavened bread a distinct festival not concerning the first passover at all, since the Israelites then ate unleavened bread of necessity, having no other, and did so for thirty days after; the commanded feast came later, commemorating a departure so hasty they had no time to leaven the dough in their troughs. Clarke says the same, the one falling on the fourteenth and the other running from the fifteenth for seven days, the first and last being holy convocations. Keil dates the instruction: from the words I brought out, Moses did not receive these directions until after the exodus, and they stand here only for their internal connection with the passover, which also reconciles the first day with the fourteenth at even, unleavened bread being eaten with the lamb.

What being cut off means nobody can say, and Clarke says so. There are thirty-six places, he counts, where the excision is threatened for neglect of a duty, and what is implied is not well known: some think a violent death, some premature, some eternal. His own view is that it means no more than separation from the rights of an Israelite, leaving the man a stranger with neither lot nor part in Israel, and inflicted only on those showing marked and obstinate contempt for divine authority. He ends with a genealogy: the punishment appears nearly the same as Christian excommunication, from which that usage seems borrowed. Calvin explains why so severe a penalty attaches to so small a thing: abstaining from leaven may be trifling in itself, as Paul teaches that bodily exercise profiteth little, yet since this ceremony kept the people's redemption in memory it was a very gross crime not to observe whatever God prescribed, the importance of the rites being estimated from their object.

The holy convocation strikes Clarke as a first: the earliest account anywhere of an assembly collected for the mere purpose of religious worship, called by God's express command and employed in a work of holiness; and the Hebrew word, he observes, answers to the Greek term we translate Church, an assembly convened by public call. Ellicott adds that the summons was made by the silver trumpets, the people gathering at the sanctuary door. Keil rejects Vitringa's rendering of the phrase as a proclamation of sanctity, giving a holy assembly for the worship of Jehovah, and notes that work needed to prepare food was allowed here though forbidden on the Sabbath, whence servile work. Wesley glosses it as a solemn day to assemble.

The removal of leaven is described from later practice. Gill reports that on the fourteenth the most diligent search was made, what was found being burnt, cast into the sea or dispersed with the wind. Clarke describes the same search, every part swept so that not a crumb remain, and adds the detail that shows how far the letter was pressed: if even a mouse was seen crossing the floor with a crumb in its mouth, the whole house was held polluted and the purification begun afresh. Leaven, he adds, was an emblem of sin, proceeding from corruption.

The stranger clause prompts Ellicott to a defence. The word means a foreigner adopted by circumcision as a full proselyte, and he thinks many of the six hundred thousand were such, having joined during the sojourn or earlier. When the exclusiveness of the Hebrews is made a charge against them, he writes, justice requires us to remember that from the first it was open to any not of Hebrew blood to share their privileges by accepting circumcision, as the Kenites and even the Gibeonites did. The contrasting phrase he renders natives of the land, a Canaan reckoned Abraham's from the first promise, so that his descendants were its expatriated inhabitants. Wesley says only that it means a proselyte.
21:
What plant struck the blood is disputed four ways. Clarke lists the renderings offered — musk, rosemary, polypody of the wall, mint, origanum, marjoram and hyssop — prefers the last, derives its name from Parkhurst as denoting cleansing qualities, and describes it as an aromatic, pungent undershrub good for the breast and lungs, supposing its medicinal virtue was probably why Scripture recommends it so particularly. Keil doubts that on geographical grounds, since it is uncertain whether the officinal hyssop grows in Syria and Arabia at all, and prefers an origanum, the Arabian zater, wild marjoram or a kind of thyme, very common there. Ellicott names a third candidate, the caper plant, called asaf by the Arabs, plentiful in Sinai and well adapted for the purpose. Gill reports the whole range and adds that rosemary seems fitter to sprinkle with than hyssop, while granting that hyssop is generally understood because the Hebrew word is so near in sound; he passes on Jarchi's rule that three stalks make a bunch, and notes that the heathens sprinkled with laurel or olive.

One word in the same verse is doubly ambiguous. The term rendered bason also means threshold, Ellicott notes, and that sense was preferred by both the Greek and the Latin; but on either reading the article is difficult, since neither had been mentioned before. Perhaps, he suggests, Moses assumed the blood was always caught in a bason and spoke of it as familiar. Against the threshold he argues that if the lamb had been sacrificed there, blood on the lintel and doorposts would scarcely have been necessary. Keil takes it simply as the vessel that caught the blood, noting that purifications elsewhere sprinkled rather than struck.

Why nobody might go out is answered four ways, one startling. Keil gives the plain reason, that on such a night there was no safety except behind the blood-stained door. Calvin makes it separation, lest they mix with the Egyptians, and a warning that they too were exposed to destruction outside the safeguard of the blood. Henry adds a practical reason, that they must not straggle and be out of the way when summoned, while insisting that the angel could perfectly well have told an Israelite from an Egyptian in the street, so that the command intimated that their safety was owing to the blood of sprinkling. Ellicott says what none of the others do: Moses seems to have given this command on his own authority, without positive divine direction, having understood that the atoning blood was the sole protection.

Who the destroyer was divides them again. Calvin holds him an angel delegated by God, and though God often executes judgment by evil angels, gathers from other passages that this was an elect angel, who also ministered the people's deliverance. Keil identifies him with the angel of Jehovah in whom God revealed himself to the patriarchs, denying he was a fallen angel, and reconciles the psalm's angels of evil by referring it to the pestilence as well. Ellicott declines the question of his nature but rules out one account, that there is any struggle between Jehovah and the destroyer, as Bishop Lowth and Redslob think; he is simply a minister, bidden to enter some houses and pass over others. Wesley refuses to decide: whether this was a good or an evil angel, we have not light to determine.

On the annual repetition Calvin draws a sharp inference from the duty of teaching. Doctrine, he says, is the life of sacraments, without which no vigour remains in them, so that lest the passover become a lifeless ceremony God enjoins that it shall not be mute; and since the paschal lamb answers to the Holy Supper, none can be duly admitted to it but those capable of being taught. Gill limits the perpetual clause to the feasts and their rites, not the sprinkling, which was peculiar to Egypt.
25:
The children's question is treated as the point of the whole institution. Clarke calls the annual service a very wise provision for keeping the deliverance in remembrance, and observes that from the remotest antiquity feasts and games have preserved the memory of grand events, so that God instituted the Sabbath to keep the creation in mind and the passover the deliverance. Calvin makes the same connection a condition of validity: the proclamation of the blessing is annexed to the sign, since otherwise it would be an empty and unmeaning proceeding, and God would have fathers proclaim it to their children, so that the knowledge of their redemption, handed down by tradition, may flourish in all ages. He adds a lexical correction, that the word some have improperly rendered work is rather used for worship, since in many passages to serve God means to worship him.

Clarke supplies a piece of later custom bearing on the question. The Jews, he reports from Calmet, never took their sons to the temple before twelve years of age, nor let them eat the flesh of any victim until they had themselves offered a sacrifice there, which they might not do before that year; and it was at this age that Joseph and Mary took the child to the temple, probably for the first time.

The prescribed answer turns on a single word. Ellicott renders the Hebrew as this is a passover-sacrifice to Jehovah, and observes that the emphatic word is passover, so that it was the meaning of this term which was especially to be explained; the explanation would necessarily involve an historical account of the institution, apt to call forth gratitude and devotion. Gill divides the sacrifice in two, eucharistical by way of thanksgiving for their safety when the firstborn of the Egyptians were slain, and propitiatory, the blood atoning for all within the house where it was sprinkled, which he takes from Aben Ezra, and typical of the atoning sacrifice of Christ.

Clarke then sets out a chain of observations connecting the rite to his own communion table. The anniversary was kept on the very day and hour of the original transaction throughout all their generations; on one of these anniversaries, and as many suppose on the very hour the lamb was first offered, Christ expired on the cross; after the destruction of Jerusalem the lamb ceased to be offered anywhere, though the anniversary is still held without sacrifice; the Lord's Supper was instituted to keep the true paschal sacrifice in commemoration, and has been observed by the whole Christian world, one very small class excepted; and as the Jews were commanded to eat the lamb, so Christ commanded his disciples to take and eat. His conclusion is that the words about an ordinance for ever are literally fulfilled, the lamb being the significator until the passion and bread and wine the continual representatives thereafter until the end of the world.

The people's response is read as more than a gesture. Calvin notes that they had professed faith and obedience from the beginning but with little constancy, being so harassed by their afflictions as to neglect their duty, and that they now correct the fault of ingratitude, not only declaring their seriousness by bowing the head but giving actual proof, since it is expressly said they diligently performed whatever was commanded. Wesley says they signified their submission to the institution as a law and their thankfulness for it as a favour and privilege. Keil puts it as appropriation, that they executed the command so that through the obedience of faith they might make the blessing of this service their own. Gill notes only that the elders departed to their several tribes.
29:
The hour is part of the blow. Keil says the stroke fell when all Egypt lay in deep sleep, to startle king and people out of their sleep of sin, and weighs whether it had a natural basis like the previous plagues: the pestilence in David's day might suggest pestilence as the means, the miracle lying in the sudden death of the firstborn of man and beast alone while Israel remained uninjured. Henry works the same detail dramatically: the three preceding nights had been made dreadful by a darkness that might be felt, so the alarm came when they hoped for one quiet night's rest; and the later plague at Jerusalem, he notes, fell by day and was less frightful. Gill notes only that they were asleep and thoughtless of danger.

Henry takes the stroke by parts. It fell on the firstborn, the joy and hope of their families, measure for measure since they had slain the Hebrews' children, and reached from the throne to the dungeon, prince and peasant standing level before God. And the cry was universal, since the Egyptians could have no help from neighbours all involved in the same calamity. Clarke supplies the ethnography behind it: no people were more remarkable for their mournings than the Egyptians, who whipped, beat and tore themselves and howled in all the excess of grief, the household running into the streets on a death; Herodotus, he notes, was once in Egypt at a solemnity and saw myriads beating themselves so.

Ellicott declines to read the next clause literally. It cannot be true that there was no house without one dead, since in half the families a daughter would have opened the womb, and in others the firstborn son would have been absent or already dead. To judge Scripture fairly, he says, we must allow for the hyperbole of Oriental expression, which substitutes universal terms for general ones; the meaning is that in most houses there was one dead, which may well be so if dependants and the pet animals that abounded in Egyptian homes are included.

Whether Pharaoh sent for Moses in person divides them three to one. Calvin thinks it not probable that God's servants were recalled into his presence, holding that he called them by sending his chief courtiers to compel their departure, which the context proves since the Egyptians immediately urged them out; nor is it absurd, he adds, to say Pharaoh called a man he had threatened with death, when he sent his nobles with the command. Clarke and Ellicott agree, Ellicott adding that the messengers were chief officials, who bowed before a Moses now recognised as very great and granted in express terms all he had ever demanded. Keil alone resists: the statement is not at variance with the earlier threat, and there is no necessity for Calvin's explanation, since a command never to appear in his sight again did not preclude sending under totally different circumstances.

The last clause draws the sharpest comment. Ellicott calls it the extreme point of Pharaoh's humiliation, that he must not only grant every demand but crave a blessing from men he had despised, thwarted and driven from his presence under threat of death; those holding the issues of life and death must, he felt, have power to bless or curse. Henry and Wesley draw the same conclusion against a rival account: he sent them out not as men hated, as the pagan historians represent, but as men feared, which his humble request plainly discovers. Calvin finds the speech a portrait: the perturbation of an alarmed man is expressed to the life, since he now takes no less precaution against delay than he had before been diligent in bargaining, and the change betrays itself, for the same God who hardened his iron heart has now broken it. Gill notes that Pharaoh at last concedes the flocks he had refused.
33:
The pressure to leave came from the whole country. Clarke puts it briefly: they felt much and feared more, wishing to be rid of a people on whose account they had been so plagued. Ellicott notes that not Pharaoh only but the Egyptian nation was anxious for an immediate departure and expedited it in every way, which facilitated their setting forth at once and accounts for their readiness to part with jewels and raiment. He corrects the English too, that lent should be gave, since the Egyptians neither expected nor wished them to return. Wesley draws the moral, that when death comes into our houses it is seasonable to think of our mortality.

What was carried away is described with unusual attention to the objects. Keil explains that the urgency forced them to take the dough unleavened, and that the garment binding the troughs was a large square cloth worn over the under-clothes; they had meant to leaven it, he adds, since the seven days' command had not yet been given, so only under pressure did they content themselves with what is elsewhere called the bread of affliction. Clarke describes the vessels from modern usage, the kneading troughs of the Arabs being small wooden bowls that afterwards serve as dishes, and suggests that bound up in their clothes may mean only wrapped in the long garment the Arabs call a hyke, a blanket like a highland plaid. Ellicott agrees on the bowls. Wesley alone declines the object, holding that the word means not kneading troughs but the lumps of unleavened paste themselves.

The mixed multitude is the chapter's open question, and each man fills it differently. Ellicott is the most candid: nothing is told us of its elements, though some may have been Egyptians impressed by the miracles and some foreigners glad to escape servitude; and Egyptian writers, in their perverted accounts of the exodus, made a multitude of foreigners take part with the Hebrews. Gill lists four motives — intermarriage, religion in proselytes of righteousness, worldly interest since Egypt was desolate, and the judgment that a people so favoured of heaven were safest company — and adds Jonathan's figure of two hundred and forty myriads. Keil takes the word as literally a mixture, a swarm of foreigners, treats their coming as a typical fulfilment of the promise that all families should be blessed in Abraham, and notes that they occupied a low position as hewers of wood whom Israel could not shake off. Henry is harshest, supposing the greatest part a rude unthinking mob that followed the crowd they knew not why, and that on learning of the forty years they quitted and returned; there were always those among the Israelites, he concludes, that were not Israelites, and there are hypocrites in the church still.

Calvin approaches the crowd from an accounting problem. Since Moses mentions no servants at the descent into Egypt, and Jacob could hardly maintain more than his children through the famine, they brought no great number down, so the mixed multitude were either Egypt's own offspring or migrants drawn there by abundance. He notes the same expression later, the mixed multitude separated from the true Israelites lest the Church be polluted by a confused admixture. And he answers an objection: if any think it absurd that ungodly men should forsake a rich habitation to become wanderers, Egypt had been so afflicted that its very poverty might easily have driven its inhabitants away.

Two notes close the passage. Gill raises a difficulty about the baking, Succoth being a desert where ovens could hardly be had, and answers that the cakes might be laid on coals and turned, or covered under hot ashes; Ellicott gives the Arab method, dough attached to the inside of a heated oven. Henry reckons the women and children at twice the six hundred thousand men, marvelling at the increase from seventy souls.
40:
The four hundred and thirty years are the chapter's hardest number, and Clarke calls the statement extremely difficult. He reports Kennicott's survey. That the descendants of Israel did not dwell so long in Egypt is easily proved; some therefore take Egypt to mean Egypt and Canaan together, but that will not close the gap; and others stretch the children of Israel to mean Israel's children, and Israel himself, and Isaac, and part of the life of Abraham. By this we do arrive at the exact sum, Kennicott grants, and by this method of reckoning we might arrive at anything but truth, which we may presume was never thus conveyed by an inspired writer.

Clarke's own answer is textual. The Samaritan Pentateuch reads that the sojourning of the children of Israel, and of their fathers, in Canaan and in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years; the Alexandrian Greek agrees; and Paul gives the same sum, reckoning from the promise made to Abraham to the giving of the law. In the mouth of these three witnesses, he says, the account is established, two clauses having dropped out of the present Hebrew. He checks it by arithmetic: twenty-five years from Abraham's entry to Isaac's birth, sixty to Jacob's, a hundred and thirty to the descent into Egypt, making two hundred and fifteen, which two hundred and fifteen in Egypt complete. Gill reports the same expansions from the Greek, the Samaritan, both Talmuds and Aben Ezra, and states flatly that Israel did not dwell in Egypt so long, nor much above two hundred years. Calvin agrees the period cannot begin from Jacob's descent, since it is very clear that from Jacob's entry to the exodus not more than two hundred and thirty years had passed.

Ellicott stands alone in defending the plain Hebrew, with two supports. He renders the clause as which they sojourned in Egypt, and points first to the prophecy that Abraham's seed should be a stranger in a land not theirs and serve them four hundred years, taking that land to be Egypt and not Canaan; then to the genealogy of Joshua, which places him in the eleventh generation from Jacob and accords well with this term, whereas the other genealogies are more or less abbreviated.

Ellicott takes the selfsame day to mean that all started on one day, some by night, some in the morning and others later, having different distances to traverse to the appointed halt.

The name given to the night divides on one word. Keil denies that it means celebration, from a root signifying to observe or honour, as Knobel held; it is preservation, from a root meaning to keep, the night being consecrated to the Lord as a preservation for all Israel in their families, because he had preserved them from the destroyer. Gill takes it as a night of observations, in which many things are marked to the honour of God, and Clarke as a night to be held in everlasting remembrance. Calvin reads the verse as a safeguard against decay: the admonition was useful, so that the Israelites should keep the legitimate use of this feast and it might not grow into a mere cold ceremony, as is often the case, but that they might exercise themselves profitably in this emblem of their redemption; and the generations of the ancient people, he notes, were ended by the coming of Christ, the shadows of the law ceasing when the Church was renewed and the Gentiles gathered into the same body. Wesley sets the two nights side by side: this first passover night was a night of the Lord much to be observed, but the last, in which Christ was betrayed, much more, when a yoke heavier than Egypt's was broken and a better land than Canaan set before us; the one a temporal deliverance, the other an eternal redemption celebrated world without end.
43:
When these supplementary rules were given is disputed. Clarke argues from the chapter's last verse that they belonged to the first passover and should be read with the earlier account, allowing that they may be particular instructions issued after the general ones but holding they all belong to that occasion. Keil says the opposite, that they were not communicated before the exodus at all, giving a reason from the narrative: only when a crowd of foreigners attached itself to Israel did a connection with foreigners arise which needed defining, particularly as regards the festival of Israel's birth as the people of God.

Clarke supplies the classification the rule depends on. All not descended from the sons of Jacob were reputed strangers, and of these there were two kinds. Proselytes of the gate would not submit to circumcision, though they acknowledged the true God, avoided idolatry and observed the seven precepts of Noah, being bound to no Mosaic institution. Proselytes of the covenant submitted to circumcision and bound themselves to all the rites of the law. The word rendered foreigner he derives from a root meaning to dwell, giving a sojourner present for traffic and belonging to neither class. Gill draws the line the same way, admitting only proselytes of righteousness; Ellicott notes that the hired servant is assumed to be a foreigner, since otherwise he would of course participate.

Keil turns the exclusion into a two-sided principle. Since Israel became the people of Jehovah by divine call and not natural descent, no foreigner could share the feast of its birth; but since in that capacity it was destined to be a blessing to all nations, the attitude toward foreigners was not to be altogether repelling, so purchased servants already incorporated as Israel's property were to be entirely incorporated by circumcision. Ellicott distinguishes slaves born in the house, circumcised on the eighth day like Israelites, from bought slaves, allowed their choice, and marks what follows: the circumcised slave was admitted to full religious equality with his master.

Calvin defends the exclusion as belonging to the nature of a sacrament. The passover was the sacred bond by which God held the elect people to himself, so a promiscuous permission to eat would have been an unworthy profanation; and among the Gentiles too none but the initiated were admitted to their rites, an absurd imitation of the true ordinance, since sacraments are testimonies of God's special favour to his Church and must not be prostituted to all comers. Circumcision was a hedge distinguishing the heathen nations from the holy race of Abraham, so that anyone wishing to keep the passover with the elect people had to be circumcised and so attach himself to the true God; but God did not refer merely to the outward sign, since all who were circumcised thereby promised to study sincere piety.

Henry runs the rule both ways. On exclusion he makes it sacramental order: none might sit at the table but those who came in by the door, and none may now approach the Lord's supper who have not first submitted to baptism, since we must be born again by the word before we can be nourished by it. On admission he finds an early indication of favour to the Gentiles, a circumcised stranger standing level with the home-born Israelite under one law for both; this was a mortification to the Jews, teaching them that it was their dedication to God and not their descent from Abraham that entitled them to their privileges. He adds that a master of a household must have all his males circumcised as well as himself. Clarke reaches the same point from the other end, that the excluded were excluded because they were not under the bond of the covenant and so had no claim on its privileges. Wesley states the condition in five words, unless he submit to be circumcised.
46:
Why no bone was to be broken gets three answers. Clarke gives a practical one, that haste left no time to separate the bones or break them for marrow, the ordinance being given lest they be tempted to spend time so; he guesses the flesh was cut off without parting the large joints, the skeleton being burnt. Ellicott gives a symbolic one, that whereas in every other victim the limbs were separated, here the animal was roasted whole and to remain whole, as a symbol of unity and a type of him through whom men are brought into unity with God. Calvin declines certainty: he is not sure why God desired no bone broken, unless this too was a sign of haste, since people at table seldom partake of the marrow except when the meal is long. He then refuses a reading his own tradition offered, fearing too much subtlety in the explanation that the virtue of Christ, represented by the bones, is not diminished while we feed on his flesh.

On the fulfilment they converge. Clarke observes that though it was universal custom to break the legs of the crucified, providence so ordered it that a bone of the true paschal Lamb was unbroken. Calvin says the same more strongly, that what God commanded concerning the lamb he chose to have openly fulfilled in his Son, so that the truth answering its type might show God would be reconciled by no other blood; and he treats the soldiers' restraint as an interference of providence, since they carried out their intention on the robbers but were held back from Christ.

Gill allows that more societies than one might eat in a house if they kept distinct and each were large enough for a whole lamb, but insists that one lamb might not be divided between houses, which he takes to denote the unity of the general assembly and the right of each congregation to a whole Christ. Clarke reads it as one family, or a neighbouring family invited if the first were too small, and connects the ban on carrying the flesh abroad with the command that none leave the house. Wesley notes that though observed in families apart it is the act of the whole congregation, and infers that the Lord's supper ought not to be neglected by any capable of celebrating it.

Clarke stops at the word law, its first occurrence, and explains it once for all. The Hebrew comes from a root signifying to aim at, teach, direct or make straight, whence its design: a system of instruction in righteousness, the fountain of every correct notion of God and the origin of all true principles of justice. He draws the political consequence that nations acknowledging this revelation have the most beneficial laws, while others have laws at once extravagantly severe and indulgent, resting on caprice rather than moral turpitude, so that government becomes oppressive and is at length overturned.

Keil reads the last two verses as hinges: the first closes the instructions by noting that Israel carried them out in after times, the second closes the account of the exodus, all that Jehovah promised being fulfilled; and though this is a concluding formula, Abenezra was so far right in connecting it with the following chapter, since such formulae link incidents, winding up what has gone before and introducing what comes. Calvin turns the note of obedience into a note about its author: not the people's promptitude is praised but the power of God in fashioning their hearts and directing their hands, so that in the darkness of the night, amid great disturbance and with nothing well prepared, they were so active and dexterous. Clarke closes on the word armies, from a root meaning to assemble in order and thence to war, finding in it the reason God is so often styled the Lord of hosts.
